6. Heard the learned counsel appearing for either side and perused the records. The point that arises for 
consideration is “whether the employee of the Respondent is entitled for reinstatement into service along with all 
benefits against the management of Department of Postal Accounts & Finance? If not to what relief the 
concerned workman is entitled?” 


7. The Petitioner Shri M. Gopinathan has stated in his claim statement that he had entered into service of the 
Respondent in the year 2008. The fact of continuous service is established by the Petitioner by adducing oral 
evidence as WW1 and filing proof of affidavit and the documents which were marked as Ex.W1 to W22. 


8. The Respondent in its reply admitted this fact that Petitioner was engaged with the Department, but stated 
that engagement was on daily wage basis and not against any MTS vacancies. The Petitioner was not a permanent 
employee and there was no employer-employee relationship exists between the Respondent and the Petitioner. The 
Respondent further stated that no appointment or engagement order was issued to the Petitioner and as per circular 
dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995, casual labourers in employment upto 01.09.1993 were only eligible to be 
conferred with temporary status and the Petitioner was not working on 01.09.1993 with the Department and 
therefore, they are not entitled for any absorption. 


9. The learned counsel for the Respondent further submits that Multi Tasking Staff Recruitment Rules, 2010 
dated 12.12.2010 is not applicable to the Petitioner. As per circular dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995 the following 
conditions must be fulfilled:- 


a) Temporary status on or before 01.09.1993; 


7146 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


b) Full time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993 & 
c) Part-time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993. 


10. The learned counsel for the Respondent contended that Petitioner was not engaged through employment 
exchange and no appointment letter was issued. He further stated that assumption of the Petitioner that he/she works 
against the post of MTS is incorrect. The learned counsel further stated that there was no relationship of employer- 
employee between the Respondent and Petitioner, hence the question of notice or protection u/s.25F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 does not arise. 


11. On behalf of the Respondent a circular dated 17.05.1989 has been filed which is marked as Ex.M1, and it 
clarifies the position of casual labourers and part-time casual labourers in para 2, which reads as under:- 


“2. It is hereby clarified that all daily wagers working in Post Offices or in RMS Offices or in Administrative Offices 
or PSD's/MMS under different designations (mazdoor casual labourer, contingent paid staff, daily wager, daily 
rated mazdoor, outsider) are to be treated as casual labourers. Those casual labourers who are engaged for a 
period of 8 hours a day should be described as full-time casual labourers. Those casual labourers who are engaged 
for a period of less than 8 hours a day should be described as part-time casual labourers. All other designations 
should be discontinued.” 


12. The Petitioner in the claim statement stated that the work was performed for a period of more than eight hours 
per day. The Respondent witness MW1 in his oral evidence nowhere stated that Petitioner did not perform the work 
about eight or more than 8 hours per day. 


13. The Respondent submitted another circular dated 11.09.1991 which is marked as Ex.M2. The subject of 
this circular is Casual Labourers (Grant of Temporary Status and Regularization) Scheme. This circular did not 
suggest date of appointment of the labourers which means this circular does not impose a condition that the casual 
labour must be in service on a particular date. 


14. The another circular issued by Respondent, Department of Posts, dated 27.11.1995 marked as Ex.M3, 
which suggests that full time casual labourers recruited after 29.11.1989 upto 10.09.1993 may also be considered 
for grant of benefits under the scheme. This circular later specified the particular date i.e., 10.09.1993. 


15. The next document marked as Ex.M5 dated 19.11.2010, which states that no casual labour shall be engaged 
in the administrative office with effect from 01.12.2010. This circular further stated that since the duties of 
waterman, watch & ward, gardening, cleaning etc. are now part of duties assigned to MTS, the existing practice of 
engaging casual labourers as waterman, gardener, watch and ward or any other category shall be dispensed with 
from 01.12.2010. The Petitioner was engaged prior to this circular dated 19.11.2010. 


16. The next document filed by the Respondent and marked as Ex.M6 is a circular issued by Ministry of 
Communications & IT, Department of Posts dated 27.01.2011 regarding filling up of vacancies on the basis of latest 
recruitment rules for the post of MTS, wherein it was directed to observe the following conditions: - 


“1) (a) 25% by appointment of Casual Labourers conferred with temporary status on the basis of Selection- 
cum-seniority failing which by, 


(2) Appointment of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 5 
hours, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(c) Appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, engaged on or before 1.9.1993, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(d) Direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time. 


, 


ii). 75% by direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time.’ 


17. This circular clearly suggests that 25% of persons must be appointed from casual labourers, who has been 
conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


18. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7147 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The 
State Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing 
arrangements, and they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts 
where the work is perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, 
why similarly placed workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 
of the Constitution of India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It 
is a constitutional discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism’”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent 
in nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader 
systemic issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig 
economy has led to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job 
security, workers and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour 
standards. Government institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even 
greater responsibility to avoid such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse 
of temporary contracts, it not only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a 
concerning precedent that can erode public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the 
present case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant 
insecurity, regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic 
disparity between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary 
employees, effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates 
exploitation but also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 


7148 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, 
and thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase 
the entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service 
and the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. 


The reference is answered accordingly.

“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the 
State governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the 
backs of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and 
year after year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The 
long-term extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and 
offends the promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a 
talisman that overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, 
and they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the 
work is perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why 
similarly placed workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of

a constitutional discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.”

term “ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent 
that daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. 
The Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify 
indefinite daily-wage status or continued unfair practices.

Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent 
in nature.

systemic issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig

job security, workers and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour 
standards. Government institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even 
greater responsibility to avoid such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in 
misuse of temporary contracts, it not only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets 
a concerning precedent that can erode public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to 
address short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations 
owed employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


dy 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those 
of regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks.

present case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant 
insecurity, regardless of the quality or duration of their service.

development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic 
disparity between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant.

employees, effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates 
exploitation but also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment.

provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security

daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers’ rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers

and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 


22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 


The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service and 
the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits.

“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that

overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that  "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 

22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days.

,

conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority.

temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority.

01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh Vs. State of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.”

Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term

daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices.

Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers’ rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 


Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment.

provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security

22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days.

following directions:-

the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits.

3५ The Petitioner has submitted proof of affidavit in support of his claim and adduced oral evidence as WW1 


and documents filed by him were marked as Ex.W1 to W22. The Respondent has also filed its proof of affidavit

6. Heard the learned counsel appearing for either side and perused the records. The point that arises for 
consideration is “whether the employee of the Respondent is entitled for reinstatement into service along with all 
benefits against the management of Department of Postal Accounts & Finance? If not to what relief the concerned 
workman is entitled?” 


7. The Petitioner Shri R.Senthamil has stated in his claim statement that he had entered into service of the 
Respondent in the year 2010. The fact of continuous service is established by the Petitioner by adducing oral 
evidence as WW1 and filing proof of affidavit and the documents which were marked as Ex.W1 to W22. 


8. The Respondent in its reply admitted this fact that Petitioner was engaged with the Department, but stated 
that engagement was on daily wage basis and not against any MTS vacancies. The Petitioner was not a permanent 
employee and there was no employer-employee relationship exists between the Respondent and the Petitioner. The 
Respondent further stated that no appointment or engagement order was issued to the Petitioner and as per circular 
dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995, casual labourers in employment upto 01.09.1993 were only eligible to be 
conferred with temporary status and the Petitioner was not working on 01.09.1993 with the Department and 
therefore, they are not entitled for any absorption. 


9. The learned counsel for the Respondent further submits that Multi Tasking Staff Recruitment Rules, 2010 
dated 12.12.2010 is not applicable to the Petitioner. As per circular dated 01.11.1995 and 08.11.1995 the following 
conditions must be fulfilled:- 


a) Temporary status on or before 01.09.1993; 
b) Full time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993 & 
c) Part-time casual labourer engaged on or before 01.09.1993. 


10. The learned counsel for the Respondent contended that Petitioner was not engaged through employment 
exchange and no appointment letter was issued. He further stated that assumption of the Petitioner that he/she works 
against the post of MTS is incorrect. The learned counsel further stated that there was no relationship of employer- 
employee between the Respondent and Petitioner, hence the question of notice or protection u/s.25F of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 does not arise. 


11. On behalf of the Respondent a circular dated 17.05.1989 has been filed which is marked as Ex.M1, and it 
clarifies the position of casual labourers and part-time casual labourers in para 2, which reads as under:- 


“2. It is hereby clarified that all daily wagers working in Post Offices or in RMS Offices or in Administrative 
Offices or PSD's/MMS under different designations (mazdoor casual labourer, contingent paid staff, daily 
wager, daily rated mazdoor, outsider) are to be treated as casual labourers. Those casual labourers who are 
engaged for a period of 8 hours a day should be described as full-time casual labourers. Those casual 
labourers who are engaged for a period of less than 8 hours a day should be described as part-time casual 
labourers. All other designations should be discontinued.” 


12. The Petitioner in the claim statement stated that the work was performed for a period of more than eight hours per 
day. The Respondent witness MW1 in his oral evidence nowhere stated that Petitioner did not perform the work 
about eight or more than 8 hours per day. 


13. The Respondent submitted another circular dated 11.09.1991 which is marked as Ex.M2. The subject of this 
circular is Casual Labourers (Grant of Temporary Status and Regularization) Scheme. This circular did not suggest 
date of appointment of the labourers which means this circular does not impose a condition that the casual labour 
must be in service on a particular date.

14. The another circular issued by Respondent, Department of Posts, dated 27.11.1995 marked as Ex.M3, 
which suggests that full time casual labourers recruited after 29.11.1989 upto 10.09.1993 may also be considered for 
grant of benefits under the scheme. This circular later specified the particular date i.e., 10.09.1993. 


15. The next document marked as Ex.MS5 dated 19.11.2010, which states that no casual labour shall be engaged 
in the administrative office with effect from 01.12.2010. This circular further stated that since the duties of waterman, 
watch & ward, gardening, cleaning etc. are now part of duties assigned to MTS, the existing practice of engaging 
casual labourers as waterman, gardener, watch and ward or any other category shall be dispensed with from 
01.12.2010. The Petitioner was engaged prior to this circular dated 19.11.2010. 


16. The next document filed by the Respondent and marked as Ex.M6 is a circular issued by Ministry of 
Communications & IT, Department of Posts dated 27.01.2011 regarding filling up of vacancies on the basis of latest 
recruitment rules for the post of MTS, wherein it was directed to observe the following conditions: - 


“1) (a) 25% by appointment of Casual Labourers conferred with temporary status on the basis of Selection- 
cum-seniority failing which by, 


(b) Appointment of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 6 
hours, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(c) Appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, engaged on or before 1.9.1993, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority failing which by, 


(d) Direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time. 
ii). 75% by direct recruitment as per the scheme circulated by the Department of Posts from time to time.” 


17. This circular clearly suggests that 25% of persons must be appointed from casual labourers, who has been 
conferred with temporary status on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. The second condition suggests appointment 
of existing Casual labourers engaged on or before 1.9.1993 working, for full hours viz. 8 hours, on the basis of 
selection-cum-seniority. The third condition suggests that appointment of existing part-time Casual Labourers, 
engaged on or before 01.09.1993, on the basis of selection-cum-seniority. 


It is true that the Respondent department never constituted any committee to select persons who conferred with 
temporary status by preparing list of selection cum seniority. 


18. All the circulars issued by Department of Posts suggest that since the Petitioner was not in service on 
01.09.1993, he/she is not entitled for absorption. In the case of Dharam Singh VsState of U.P & Another in Civil 
Appeal No.8558 of 2018 dated 19.08.2025, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as_under:- 


“17. Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the State 
governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the backs 
of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year after 
year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long-term 
extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


18. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that "ad-hocism" thrives where administration is opaque. The State 
Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing arrangements, and 
they must explain, with evidence. why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts where the work is 
perennial. If "constraint" is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, why similarly placed 
workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is a constitutional 
discipline that should inform every decision affecting those who keep public offices running.” 


19. In the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India in SLP No.5580 of 2024 (2024) SCC online 3826 and Shripal & 
Another Vs. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (2025) SCC online 221, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that long-term 
“ad hocism”, is denial of basic parity. The Hon'ble Supreme Court denied the contention of the Respondent that 
daily wagers and temporary employees cannot claim permanent absorption in the absence of statutory Rules. The 
Hon’ble Court further stated that the alleged asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite 
daily-wage status or continued unfair practices. 


20. In the present case, the Petitioner has continuously rendered services over several years . The Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held in the case of Shripal & Another (supra) that Indian Labour Law is 


strongly disfavors perpetual daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances, where the work is permanent in 
nature. 


7184 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


21. Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo Vs. Union of India (supra) has observed as under:- 


"22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers' rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, workers 
and and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid 
such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not 
only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode 
public trust in governmental operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security. and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 
Arbitrary Temporary Termination: employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the present 
case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant insecurity, 
regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 
Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally significant. 
Using Outsourcing as Institutions Shield: to increasingly resort outsourcing roles performed by temporary employees, 
effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates exploitation but 
also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 
Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as pension, 
provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social security 
subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances." 
22. The learned counsel for the Respondent argued that no appointment order was issued to the Petitioner, and 
thus no permanent status is allowable to the Petitioner. But the non-issuance of appointment order does not erase the 
entitlement of the Petitioner since the Petitioner has worked for several years and not days. 

AWARD 

In view of the foregoing discussion, the appeal filed by the Petitioner is liable to be allowed with the 
following directions:- 

The Petitioner’s service shall stand regularized with effect from the date of removal/denial from service and 
the Petitioner shall be reinstated into service within a period of three months with 50% back wages and 
consequential & other attendant benefits. 

The reference is answered accordingly. 
Record be consigned to the record room.

1. This Petition has been filed by the Petitioner workman under section 2(A) (2) of Industrial Dispute 
Act 1947 with the prayer to set aside his dismissal order dated 277 May 2016 passed by the Respondent Management 
and to direct the Respondent to reinstate Petitioner in the service with continuity of service with all back wages and 
all other attendant benefits. 


2. The facts in brief culled out from the petition are that the Petitioner workman was appointed as a Toll 
Collector in Swarna Tollway Private Limited Organization on 2" December 2004. 


Further, Petitioner submitted that he was place under suspension with issuing Charge sheet on 9" September 
2015, and without considering his explanation Respondent has dismissed him vide order dated 27" May 2016. 
Further, Petitioner submitted that on 1“ September 2015 he was member of Swarna Toll Employees Union, and he 
went to Budanam Base Camp office to meet with office bearer of the union and number of employees, union 
president and some other office bearers were also present at Budanam base camp office to meet with the COM to 
represent their demands. When the union leader entered into the Chamber of COM. Other employees were waiting 
outside camp office of COM and Some discussions took place between Union leaders and the management. As per 
petitioner COM did not consider the lawful demands of the employees and union leaders came outside and explained 
to other employees. Since lawful demands were not considered by the Respondent COM, Union leaders and 
employees expressed their protest against the Respondent Management by shouting slogans. COM and other 
managers foisted a false case against the petitioner and rest of the employees present there at Chillakuru Police 
Station. The Police authority registered a case in Crime No.154/2015 against the 28 employees and they sent the 
there employees to remand. The Chief of operation and maintenance and other Toll Managers made a complaint what 
has been alleged in the charge sheet. Further, Petitioner stated that he was no way concerned in the said incident there 
was no specific allegation against him. The allegations made against all the 28 employees are in common Petitioner 
contended that before issuing charge sheet, the copy of complaint was not supplied to him to submit his explanation 
and he never committed any misconduct of willful in subordination or disobedience with the lawful and reasonable 
order of superior. He never damage the employer’s business or property and did not instigate co-workman to 
misbehave with official of Management. He never committed any act subversive of discipline and I never assaulted 
and grievously hurting the management as alleged in the charge sheet. Further, Petitioner submitted that enquiry has 
been conducted by the enquiry officer into the allegations without following principle of natural justice. There was no 
corroborative evidence to prove the guilt of Petitioner and only management witness were examined in the enquiry. 
The management witness nowhere has stated that what acts, and omission committed by C.S.E and, there was no legal 
evidence to prove the allegations against C.S.E. Thus, enquiry officer has also failed to bring home the guilt of C.S.E 
and gave common findings of all the 28 C.S.E which is not legal. Enquiry officer has conducted enquiry an empty 
formality, and submitted his report holding that the allegation are proved. The procedure followed by the enquiry 
office, and enquiry findings are not fair, proper and not maintainable under law. Respondent management had issued 
show cause notice to petitioner and without considering his explanation the Respondent management passed his 
dismissal order on 27-05-2016 that is not sustainable under law. 


Further, Petitioner submitted that the allegation leveled against him were false and fabricated and there was 
no specific allegation against him for violation of any acts or omissions. All the common allegations has been made 
against the 28 employees. There was no willful in subordination or disobedience of instruction in connection with the 
order of the superior and no damages done with the employer business or property. There was no unprovoked 
behavior with customers riotous disorderly or indecent behavior in premises of the establishment. There was no act 
subversive of discipline. It is submitted that Petitioner had not committed due serious misconduct to dismiss him from 
service. Further it is submitted that Petitioner filed the ID No 14 of 2017 before the labour Court Guntur and labour 
court passed the order dated 31 -8-2019 thereby rejecting the petition on the ground of lack jurisdiction. Therefore, 
any delay in filing the appeal is on account of COVID-19 pandemic situations prevailing all over the world. 
Therefore, prayed to set aside the order dated 27-05-2016 passed by Respondent and to reinstate the Petitioner in the 
service,

unnecessarily has been made party in the present Petition as there is no employe relationship between the Petitioner 
and Respondent No.1. Further, it is submitted that the Respondent No.1 is neither concerned nor related to allegation 
made in the petition hence denied. Respondent has unnecessarily been made party to the present proceeding and

Respondent No. 2 and 3 has filed counter and has contended there in that present petition has been filed by

Findings: - 
Issue No. I 


The Departmental inquiry conducted against the Workman Sri. Daggu Sathish has been held legal and valid, 
by this court vide order dated 117 November 2024. 


Thus, issue is decided accordingly. 
Issue No. II 


In this context, Respondent No.2 and 3 contended that the present Industrial Dispute has been raised by the 
Petitioner on 2" August 2021 after the lapse of five years from the date of his dismissal order dated 27" May 2016. 
Therefore, in view of the provision contained under section 2-A (3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, this claim could be 
filed by the Petitioner before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or 
otherwise termination of service as specified in (1) of section 2-A. Therefore, the present claim Petition raising the 
Industrial Dispute by Petitioner under section 2A (2) of the ID Act, is barred by limitation. 


The perusal of claim petition goes to reveals that Petitioner has raised the Industrial Dispute against his dismissal 
order, dated 30" august 2016 passed the by the Respondent Management by filing claim petition in the year 2021. In 
the para 11 of claim petition, Petitioner has averred that against his termination order, he approached to the Deputy 
Labour Commissioner of Labor, Nellore for cancellation and same was dismissed without considering the merit. 
Thereafter, he filed petition before Labour court, Guntur, which got registered as ID Number 158/2016. Labour 
Court, Guntur, vide order dated 317 August 2019, has returned his petition on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. 
Thereafter due to COVID-19 pandemic situation Petitioner could not approach this court within time. Petitioner has 
also filed the copy of the order dated 31-08-2019 passed by the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Guntur, in ID no. 
158/2016, whereby Labour Court Guntur has returned petition of the Petitioner for presentation before the appropriate 
court of jurisdiction. It is established fact that in the year 2020, there was a prevailing situation of COVID-19 
pandemic and Petitioner was not able to approach this court to present petition at Hyderabad. Thus, Petitioner has 
furnished cogent and sufficient explanation of delay in filing the present petition and same is not fatal to present 
Industrial Dispute. Therefore, in view of the above present petition raising the Industrial Dispute under section 2-A 
(2) of the ID Act, against the dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 is not barred by limitation. Issue is decided in favor of 
the Petitioner. 


Issue No. III 


The perusal of record goes to reveal that in this claim petition, petitioner has challenged his dismissal order 
dated 30" August 2016, passed by Respondent Management on the grounds alleged in petition. Furthermore, perusal 
of the record of inquiry proceeding along with inquiry report, goes to reveal that the Petitioner was given fair 
opportunity of hearing at every stage of proceedings, which he availed, without raising any objection complaining of 
any prejudice of any nature caused to him before the inquiry officer at any point of time. Further, it is noticed that the 
Workman CSC received all the documents filed and relied upon by the Respondent management in support of the 
charge sheet, and CSC workman also filed a reply, cross-examined the management witnesses, and also examined 
himself as a witness in defense. Thus, the workman CSC has participated in the inquiry proceeding at every stage. 
Inquiry officer, on appreciation of evidence recorded in inquiry has submitted his reasoned report holding the 
workman guilty of the charges. Therefore, in the opinion of the court, no case is made out to hold that the domestic 
inquiry suffers from any procedural lapses or was conducted in violation of principles of natural justice, thereby 
causing any prejudice to the rights of the Petitioner. Moreover, validity and legality of the domestic inquiry has been 
upheld by the court vide order dated 11" November 2024. Thus, the plea of the Petitioner that the domestic inquiry 
was conducted against the Petitioner in violation of principle of natural justice is untenable. 


It is settled law that once it is held that the domestic inquiry is legal and proper, the next question arises for 
consideration whether the punishment imposed on the Petitioner is just and legal, or it is disproportionate to the 
gravity of the charges. Petitioner has challenged his dismissal order on the ground that the allegations leveled against 
him are false and fabricated, and during the inquiry no other employee as witness was examined to prove the charges 
and there was no corroborating evidence to prove the guilt and only that management witness were examined in the 
inquiry. Further, it is contended that there was no legal evidence before enquiry to prove the allegations, and the 
inquiry officer had also failed to bring home the charge against the Petitioner. Further, Petitioner has strenuously 
argued that the inquiry officer conducted the inquiry as empty formality and without having any valid and legal 
evidence and came to the conclusion that allegations are proved. Further, it is urged Petitioner that had not committed 
any misconduct as alleged in the charge sheet, and there was no evidence of loss of revenue to the corporation. 
Further, it is contended that there was no willful insubordination or disobedience of instructions in connection with 
the orders of the superior. There was no damage or dishonesty in connection with the employer’s business or 
property, and Petitioner was not involved in unprovoked misbehavior with the customer, riotous, disorderly, or 
indecent behavior in the premises of the establishment. Lastly it is pleaded that the dismissal order passed by the 
Respondent management is grossly disproportionate to the gravity of the offense, and same is liable to be set aside. In 
view of plea taken by Petitioner, peruse the record of inquiry proceeding.

11. Further, domestic inquiry against CSE has been conducted strictly in accordance with the principle of natural 
justice and workman CSE has been found guilty of grave and serious acts of misconduct. Thus, finding of the inquiry 
officer is based on of oral and documentary evidence recorded during enquiry and report of inquiry officer do not 
suffers from any illegality or perversely. The inquiry officer report goes to reveal that on 1-09-2015 CSE workman, 
has committed the misconduct of physical assault to the official of Respondent Management and he has been rightly 
held guilty of committing misconduct. The details of specific acts of misconduct allegedly committed by the 
Petitioner along with other co-workman on 1-09-2015 including physical assault on Respondent staff are as follows: - 


That the Petitioner workman has physically assaulted Mr. Hari Pandu Ranga Swamy Madasu, the Chief 
Operations and Maintenance, thereby causing grievous injuries. The act not only endangered the safety of a senior 
official but also disrupted the discipline and harmony of the workplace. Further, Petitioner workman actively 
participated in a riotous mob attack, leading to the damage of company property, and creating an atmosphere of fear 
and disorder within the establishment. Such conduct undermines the safety and security of the workplace environment 
and lastly. The Petitioner workman exhibited willful insubordination by disobeying lawful and reasonable orders of 
his superiors. Furthermore, he threatened senior officials, displaying gross indiscipline and a blatant disregard for the 
hierarchical structure and decorum expected within the organization. 


12. The findings of enquiry officer are based on cogent and credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and 
documentary proof. The enquiry was conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, providing the 
Petitioner ample opportunity to defend himself. Thus, the aforementioned acts committed by the Petitioner workman 
squarely fall under the category of serious misconduct as defined under Clauses 19(a), (c), (d) and (e) of the Andhra 
Pradesh Shops and establishments Rules, 1990. 


Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is 
not condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and 
appropriate action. 


13. Respondent has relied upon the few decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court which are relevant to the point and 
discussed as here under: -

Manager, was justified, and interference by the Labour Court under Section 11-A of the ID Act was disapproved and

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M.P, Electricity Board Vs. Jagdish Chandra Sharma - order (2005) 3 SCC

impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with law.” 


In the case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd — (2008) 5 SCC 554, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and Rubber Co. Vs. 
The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere 
therewith. In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to 
a conclusion that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested 
otherwise but it is another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere 
hypothesis. It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the 
Act although is a wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and 
analyze the evidence but what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal 
and proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman 
had Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, 
which was awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the 
punishment was awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record." 


(g) The Supreme Court in the case of Northeastern Karnataka RTC Vs. Ashappa 2006 (5) SCC 137 reaffirmed 
that the Tribunal must not lightly interfere with the employer's disciplinary decisions and reiterated the "shockingly 
disproportionate" standard. 


(h) In Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka (cupra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
clarified that the days of automatic sympathy towards the workman are over, and that discipline must be maintained at 
all costs in light of contemporary industrial conditions. The Tribunal's power to substitute the employer's decision 
must be exercised with restraint. 


(i) In the case of Muriadih Colliery (Supra) & Krishnakali Tea 


Estate (Supra), the Apex Court expressly held that interference by Labour Courts with dismissal orders passed for

Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Honorable Apex Court as discussed above, there is ample 
oral and documentary evidence on record to substantiate the charges against the petitioner workman, and it cannot be

14. As regard the plea of the petitioner workman that Respondent Management has victimize him due to the being 
member of the union and also for raising the demand related to welfare of the workman.

In this context, Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Iron 
Works versus Bhagobhai Balubhai Patel, 1976 SCC page 518. Therein Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
legal test for establishing the plea of victimization as discussed here under: - 


"11. The onus of establishing plea of victimisation will be upon the person pleading 


it. Since a charge of victimisation is a serious matter reflecting, to a degree, subjective upon the attitude of 
the employer evidenced by acts and conduct, it has to be established by safe and sure evidence. Mere allegations, 
vague suggestions and insinuations are not enough. All particulars of the charge brought out, if believed, must be 
weighed by the Tribunal and a conclusion should be reached on a totality of the evidence produced." 


The Apex Court further held: 


"12. Once, in the opinion of the Tribunal a gross misconduct is established, as required, on legal evidence either in a 
fairly conducted domestic enquiry or before the Tribunal on merits, the plea of victimisation will not carry the case of 
the employee any further. A proved misconduct is antithesis of victimisation as understood in industrial relations." 


15. Thus, in view of the principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court, as discussed above the petitioner workman has 
failed to produce any evidence in support of the plea that the action of Respondent management in dismissing him 
from service is victimization of the petitioner workman. The petitioner workman has failed to discharge his burden of

16. As regard the plea of the petitioner that they he has been acquitted from the criminal trial by court in respect of 
the alleged acts of misconduct. In this context, the decision of Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Deputy 
Inspector General of Police versus Sethu . Thiruvan, 2013 SCC page 598 is relevant, wherein Honorable Apex Court 
have held that mere acquittal in a criminal trial does not nullify or override the finding of a valid domestic inquiry. 
Further, Honorable Apex Court held that the standard of proof in a criminal trial is proof beyond reasonable doubt, 
whereas in a domestic inquiry it is only preponderance of the probability. 


In the case of Commissioner of Police vs Narendra Singh, 2006 SCC page 265, Honorable Apex Court held 
that the disciplinary proceeding can proceed independently and that an employee can be dismissed from service based 
on finding of a department inquiry even if no conviction is recorded in the criminal trial. The finding in the inquiry 
against the workman is based on credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and documentary records and 
same does not warrant any interference. 


17. Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Employers Management West Bokaro Gallery Colly of TISCO Limited 
vs Concern Workman Ram Prakash Singh, 2008 LLR, page 432, 


“16. In U.P State Road Transport Corporation Vinod Kumar, 2007 (13) SCALE 690 this Court again observed that in 
the absence of a challenge to the legality or fairness of the domestic enquiry the Court should be reluctant to either 
interfere with the finding recorded by the Enquiry officer or the punishment awarded by the Punishing Authority. 


17. After going through the order of the industrial Tribunal, were are of the opinion that the Tribunal has interfered 
with the findings recorded by the domestic. Tribunal as if it was the appellate Tribunal. There was evidence present 
on record regarding indecent riotous and disorderly behavior of the Respondent towards his superiors. The 
management witness who were present at the scene of occurrence have unequivocally deposed about the misbehavior 
of the Respondent towards his superiors. Their evidence has been discarded by the Tribunals by observing that in the 
absence of independent evidence, the statements of the workmen who were present at the scene of occurrence could 
not be believed. Industrial Tribunal tell in error in discarding the evidence produce by the management only because 
the independent witnesses were not produce them. It is possible that at the time of occurrence, only the workers of the 
Management and the persons who were truing to put up the constructions dependent evidence was available. 
Statements of the fellow workmen had established the misconduct of the Respondent. Enquiry officer accepted the 
testimony of the witness produced by the management who had clearly implicated the Respondent. It was a legitimate 
conclusion which could be arrived at and it would not be open to the industrial Tribunal to substitute the said opinion 
by its own opinion. 


19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing 
Authority by observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has 
repeatedly had been held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of 
a disciplinary proceeding against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a 
criminal case is different from the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof 
beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the 
evidence on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one 
arrived at by the domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal.

is no legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove

18. Further, as regard the appreciation and evaluation of the evidence in matter of domestic inquiry, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court, in the case of State of Rajasthan and others Vs Him Singh, Civil Appeal Number 3340 of 2020, 
date of decision: 29th October 2021, has laid down the principles extracted as here under: - 


“Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of 
evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a 
criminal trial, of proof be yond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. 
Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the 
spectrum is founded on deference and autonomy -deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact- 
finding authority and autonomy of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. Al the other 
end of the spectrum is the principle that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are 
based on no evidence or when they suffer from perversity. 


To determine whether the finding in a disciplinary inquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of 
scrutiny is undertaken. That is to satisfy the conscience of the courts that there is some evidence to support the charge 
of misconduct and to guard against perversity, but this does not allow the court to re- appreciate evidentiary findings 
in a disciplinary enquiry or to substitute a view which appears lo the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would 
offend the first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense 
without which the judges' craft is in vain.” 


19. In the case of Hombe Gouda Education Trust Vs State of Karnataka, 2006 SCC, page 430: Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held that assaulting a superior at a workplace amount to an act of gross indiscipline. The respondent is a 
teacher. Even under grave provocation, a teacher is not expected to abuse the head of the institution in a filthy 
language and assault him with a chappal. punishment of dismissal from service, therefore, cannot be said to be 
wholly disproportionate so as to shock one's conscience. Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a person, when 
dismissed from service, is put to great hardship, but that would not mean that a grave misconduct (assault on superior 
at workplace) should go unpunished. Maintenance of discipline of an institution is equally important. 


20.Further, In the case of MP Electricity Board Vs Jagdish Sharma, 2005 SCC, page 401, Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held: 


"9. In the case on hand, the employee has been found guilty of hitting and injuring his superior officer at the 
workplace obviously in the breach of Presence of other employees This clearly amounted in an discipline in the 
organisation Discipline at the workplace organisation like the employer herein, is the sine qua non for the efficient 
working of the organisation, when an employee breaches such discipline and the employer terminates his services it 
is not open to a Labour Court of an Industrial Tribunal to take view that the punishment awarded is shockingly 
disproportionate to the charge proved. We have already 


referred to the views of this Court. To quote Jack Chan, 


‘Discipline is a form of civilly responsible behaviour which helps maintain social order and contributes to 
the preservation, if not advancement, of collective interests of society at large.’ 


Obviously, this idea is more relevant in considering the working of an organisation like the employer herein or an 
industrial undertaking. Obedience to authority in a workplace is not slavery. It is rot violative of one's natural rights. It 
is essential for the prosperity of the organisation as well as that of its employee’s. When in such a situation, a 
punishment of termination is awarded for hitting and injuring a superior officer supervising the work of the employee, 
with no extenuating circumstance established, it cannot be said to be not justified. It cannot certainly be termed 
unduly harsh or disproportionate. The Labour Court and the High Court in this case totally misdirected themselves 
while exercising their jurisdiction. The Industrial Court made the correct approach and came to the right conclusion." 


21. Further, in the case of Ajit Kumar Nag Vs Indian Oil Corporation Limited, 2005 SCC page 764, the 
Honorable Supreme Court has held, in a three-judge bench, in paragraph 56, "It is well settled that the burden of 
proving malafide is on the person making the allegation, and the burden is very heavy. There is every presumption in

the allegations of malafide are often more easily made than made out, and the very seriousness of such allegations 
demands proof of a high degree of credibility." 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that assault, intimidation are penal offences. A workman indulging in 
commission of criminal offenses should not be spared only because he happens to be a union leader. The act does not

despite the fact that the management is precluded from adducing any fresh evidence before the labor court. A union 
leader does not enjoy immunity from being proceeded with in a case of misconduct.

24(1). The Labour Court also found that the alleged assault did not In our amount to misconduct under Standing

24. Thus, in view of the foregone discussion and law laid down by the apex court as discussed above, in the instant 
matter all the charges framed and proved in domestic inquiry against the workman being serious and grave in nature 
and stands proved by oral and documentary evidence recorded and produced bin the inquiry. Further, the evidence 
produced by the management before inquiry is legal and admissible as per principle of preponderance of probability 
laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court in its various decisions as discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award.

disproportionate to the gravity of the charges. Thus, the punishment of dismissal of the workman is proportionate to
