19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing 
Authority by observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has 
repeatedly had been held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of 
a disciplinary proceeding against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a 
criminal case is different from the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof 
beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the 
evidence on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one 
arrived at by the domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal. 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the apex court, as discussed above, the plea of the petitioner that there 
is no legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove 
the guilt of the workman in the alleged misconduct. 


16. Further, as regard the appreciation and evaluation of the evidence in matter of domestic inquiry, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court, in the case of State of Rajasthan and others Vs Him Singh, Civil Appeal Number 3340 of 2020, 
date of decision: 29th October 2021, has laid down the principles extracted as here under: - 


“Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of 
evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a 
criminal trial, of proof be yond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. 
Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the 
spectrum is founded on deference and autonomy -deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact- 
finding authority and autonomy of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. Al the other 
end of the spectrum is the principle that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are 
based on no evidence or when they suffer from perversity. 


To determine whether the finding in a disciplinary inquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of 
scrutiny is undertaken. That is to satisfy the conscience of the courts that there is some evidence to support the charge 
of misconduct and to guard against perversity, but this does not allow the court to re- appreciate evidentiary findings 
in a disciplinary enquiry or to substitute a view which appears lo the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would 
offend the first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense 
without which the judges' craft is in vain.” 


17. In the case of Hombe Gouda Education Trust Vs State of Karnataka, 2006 SCC, page 430: Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held that assaulting a superior at a workplace amount to an act of gross indiscipline. The respondent is a 
teacher. Even under grave provocation, a teacher is not expected to abuse the head of the institution in a filthy 
language and assault him with a chappal. punishment of dismissal from service, therefore, cannot be said to be 
wholly disproportionate so as to shock one's conscience. Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a person, when 
dismissed from service, is put to great hardship, but that would not mean that a grave misconduct (assault on superior 
at workplace) should go unpunished. Maintenance of discipline of an institution is equally important. 


18. Further, In the case of MP Electricity Board Vs Jagdish Sharma, 2005 SCC, page 401, Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held: 


"9. In the case on hand, the employee has been found guilty of hitting and injuring his superior officer at the 
workplace obviously in the breach of Presence of other employees This clearly amounted in an discipline in the 
organisation Discipline at the workplace organisation like the employer herein, is the sine qua non for the efficient 
working of the organisation, when an employee breaches such discipline and the employer terminates his services it 
is not open to a Labour Court of an Industrial Tribunal to take view that the punishment awarded is shockingly 
disproportionate to the charge proved. We have already 


referred to the views of this Court. To quote Jack Chan, 


‘Discipline is a form of civilly responsible behaviour which helps maintain social order and contributes to 
the preservation, if not advancement, of collective interests of society at large.’ 


Obviously, this idea is more relevant in considering the working of an organisation like the employer herein or an 
industrial undertaking. Obedience to authority in a workplace is not slavery. It is rot violative of one's natural rights. It 
is essential for the prosperity of the organisation as well as that of its employee’s. When in such a situation, a 
punishment of termination is awarded for hitting and injuring a superior officer supervising the work of the employee, 
with no extenuating circumstance established, it cannot be said to be not justified. It cannot certainly be termed 
unduly harsh or disproportionate. The Labour Court and the High Court in this case totally misdirected themselves 
while exercising their jurisdiction. The Industrial Court made the correct approach and came to the right conclusion."

19. Further, in the case of Ajit Kumar Nag Vs Indian Oil Corporation Limited, 2005 SCC page 764, the 
Honorable Supreme Court has held, in a three-judge bench, in paragraph 56, "It is well settled that the burden of 
proving malafide is on the person making the allegation, and the burden is very heavy. There is every presumption in 
favor of the administration that the power has been exercised bona fide and in good faith. It is to be remembered that 
the allegations of malafide are often more easily made than made out, and the very seriousness of such allegations 
demands proof of a high degree of credibility." 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that assault, intimidation are penal offences. A workman indulging in 
commission of criminal offenses should not be spared only because he happens to be a union leader. The act does not 
encourage indiscipline. It will be a matter of some concern if the opinion of the inquiry officer can be totally ignored, 
despite the fact that the management is precluded from adducing any fresh evidence before the labor court. A union 
leader does not enjoy immunity from being proceeded with in a case of misconduct. 


20. In the case of D. Mulchandani Electric and Radio Industries Limited Vs Workman, 1975 Supreme Court Cases 
page 731, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held: 


establishment 


“Tt was not disputed before us that the allegation of assault, if proved, would be an act subversive of discipline: what 
was contended on behalf of the respondent was between Thana and the premises was that the alleged assault having 
taken place in the train Mulund which was obviously outside the or precincts of the establishment, was not covered by 
Standing Order. 


24(1). The Labour Court also found that the alleged assault did not In our amount to misconduct under Standing 
Order 24(1) which, it was held was restricted to acts and omissions inside the premises of the establish opinion, Lon a 
plain reading of the clause, the words "within the premises or precincts of the establishment" refer not to the place 
where the act which is subversive of discipline or good behaviour is committed but where the consequence of such an 
act manifests itself. In other words, an act, wherever committed, if it has the effect of sub- verting discipline or good 
behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment, will amount to misconduct under Standing Order 
24(1) We are unable to agree that Standing Order 24(1) leaves out of its scone an act committed outside though it may 
result in subversion of discipline or good behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment in question. 
Such a construction in our view would be quite unreasonable.” 


21. In the case of State bank of Bikaner and Jaipur vs Nemi Channel via 2011 Supreme Court cases page 580 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held that subsequent acquittal by criminal court will not in any way render completed 
discipline proceeding invalid, nor affect the validity of finding of the guilt and consequential punishment. 


22. Thus, in view of the foregone discussion and law laid down by the apex court as discussed above, in the instant 
matter all the charges framed and proved in domestic inquiry against the workman being serious and grave in nature 
and stands proved by oral and documentary evidence recorded and produced in the inquiry. Further the evidence 
produced by the management before inquiry is legal and admissible as per principle of preponderance of probability 
laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court in its various documents as discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award. 
Therefore, order of dismissal of Petitioner workman cannot be faulted with, nor it can be said to be in any way 
disproportionate to the gravity of the charges. Thus, the punishment of dismissal of the workman is proportionate to 
the gravity of the charges, and hence deserve to be upheld. Thus, the action of the respondent management in 
dismissing the services of the workman is held legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the workman and in favor of the respondent management. 
Issue No: IV 


In view of foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, वा and III, I am of the considered opinion 
that the action of Respondent management in dismissing the Petitioner from service vide order dated 30-08-2016 is

Petitioner and the action of Respondent Management is held legal and justified and liable to be confirmed.

In view of the foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, II, III, and IV, the action of Respondent 
Management in dismissing the service of the Petitioner workman vide order dated 30-08-2016 is held legal and

Findings: - 
Issue No. I 


The Departmental inquiry conducted against the Workman Sri. Daggu Sathish has been held legal and valid, 
by this court vide order dated 117 November 2024.

Issue No. II 


In this context, Respondent No.2 and 3 contended that the present Industrial Dispute has been raised by the 
Petitioner on 2" August 2021 after the lapse of five years from the date of his dismissal order dated 27" May 2016. 
Therefore, in view of the provision contained under section 2-A (3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, this claim could be 
filed by the Petitioner before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or 
otherwise termination of service as specified in (1) of section 2-A. Therefore, the present claim Petition raising the 
Industrial Dispute by Petitioner under section 2A (2) of the ID Act, is barred by limitation. 


The perusal of claim petition goes to reveals that Petitioner has raised the Industrial Dispute against his dismissal 
order, dated 30" august 2016 passed the by the Respondent Management by filing claim petition in the year 2021. In 
the para 11 of claim petition, Petitioner has averred that against his termination order, he approached to the Deputy 
Labour Commissioner of Labor, Nellore for cancellation and same was dismissed without considering the merit. 
Thereafter, he filed petition before Labour court, Guntur, which got registered as ID Number 199/2016. Labour 
Court, Guntur, vide order dated 317 August 2019, has returned his petition on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. 
Thereafter due to COVID-19 pandemic situation Petitioner could not approach this court within time. Petitioner has 
also filed the copy of the order dated 31-08-2019 passed by the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Guntur, in ID no. 
199/2016, whereby Labour Court Guntur has returned petition of the Petitioner for presentation before the appropriate 
court of jurisdiction. It is established fact that in the year 2020, there was a prevailing situation of COVID-19 
pandemic and Petitioner was not able to approach this court to present petition at Hyderabad. Thus, Petitioner has 
furnished cogent and sufficient explanation of delay in filing the present petition and same is not fatal to present 
Industrial Dispute. Therefore, in view of the above present petition raising the Industrial Dispute under section 2-A 
(2) of the ID Act, against the dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 is not barred by limitation. Issue is decided in favor of 
the Petitioner. 


Issue No. III 


The perusal of record goes to reveal that in this claim petition, petitioner has challenged his dismissal order 
dated 30" August 2016, passed by Respondent Management on the grounds alleged in petition. Furthermore, perusal 
of the record of inquiry proceeding along with inquiry report, goes to reveal that the Petitioner was given fair 
opportunity of hearing at every stage of proceedings, which he availed, without raising any objection complaining of 
any prejudice of any nature caused to him before the inquiry officer at any point of time. Further, it is noticed that the 
Workman CSC received all the documents filed and relied upon by the Respondent management in support of the 
charge sheet, and CSC workman also filed a reply, cross-examined the management witnesses, and also examined 
himself as a witness in defense. Thus, the workman CSC has participated in the inquiry proceeding at every stage. 
Inquiry officer, on appreciation of evidence recorded in inquiry has submitted his reasoned report holding the

workman guilty of the charges. Therefore, in the opinion of the court, no case is made out to hold that the domestic

upheld by the court vide order dated 117 November 2024. Thus, the plea of the Petitioner that the domestic inquiry

It is settled law that once it is held that the domestic inquiry is legal and proper, the next question arises for

10. The findings of enquiry officer are based on cogent and credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and 
documentary proof. The enquiry was conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, providing the 
Petitioner ample opportunity to defend himself. Thus, the aforementioned acts committed by the Petitioner workman 
squarely fall under the category of serious misconduct as defined under Clauses 19(a), (c), (d) and (e) of the Andhra 
Pradesh Shops and establishments Rules, 1990. 


Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is 
not condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and 
appropriate action.

cannot be taken lightly, and the punishment of dismissal was warranted to preserve discipline and safety at the 
workplace. 


(b) Similarly, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Muriadih Colliery Vs. Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union - 
(2005) 3 SCC 331, held that the dismissal of employees who participated in a violent mob attack, causing 
injury to the General Manager, was justified, and interference by the Labour Court under Section 11-A of the 
ID Act was disapproved and the punishment proportionate to the misconduct. was upheld. 


(c) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M.P, Electricity Board Vs. Jagdish Chandra Sharma - order (2005) 
3 SCC 401. of dismissal of a Workman who assaulted a senior officer, restored the decision of the Industrial 
Court, thereby reiterating that acts of violence by employees, particularly against their superiors, must be 
dealt with strictly and are not open to lenient treatment. The reinstatement ordered by the Labour Court was 
reversed, affirming the employer's authority to maintain discipline through dismissal. 


(d) In the case of Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka - (2006) 1 


SSC 430, the Hon’ble Supreme Court underscored the importance of workplace discipline and held that even 
provoked assault on a superior, amounts to gross indiscipline. The Court stated: "30. In view of the change in 
economic policy of the country, it may not now be proper to allow the employees to break the discipline with 
impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with 
law.” 


(e) In the case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd - (2008) 5 SCC 554, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and 
Rubber Co. Vs. The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere 
therewith. In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to 
a conclusion that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested 
otherwise but it is another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere 
hypothesis. It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the 
Act although is a wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and 
analyze the evidence but what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal 
and proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman 
had Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, 
which was awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the 
punishment was awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record." 


(g) The Supreme Court in the case of Northeastern Karnataka RTC Vs. Ashappa 2006 (5) SCC 137 reaffirmed 
that the Tribunal must not lightly interfere with the employer's disciplinary decisions and reiterated the "shockingly 
disproportionate" standard. 


(h) In Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka (cupra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
clarified that the days of automatic sympathy towards the workman are over, and that discipline must be maintained at 
all costs in light of contemporary industrial conditions. The Tribunal's power to substitute the employer's decision 
must be exercised with restraint. 


(i) In the case of Muriadih Colliery (Supra) & Krishnakali Tea 


Estate (Supra), the Apex Court expressly held that interference by Labour Courts with dismissal orders passed for 
acts involving violence and assault was not permissible under section 11-A of the ID Act, as the punishment was not 
disproportionate.

Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Honorable Apex Court as discussed above, there is ample 
oral and documentary evidence on record to substantiate the charges against the petitioner workman, and it cannot be 
said that the order of dismissal of Petitioner is perverse or shockingly disproportionate. 


12. As regard the plea of the petitioner workman that Respondent Management has victimize him due to the being 
member of the union and also for raising the demand related to welfare of the workman. 


In this context, Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Iron 
Works versus Bhagobhai Balubhai Patel, 1976 SCC page 518. Therein Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
legal test for establishing the plea of victimization as discussed here under: - 


"11. The onus of establishing plea of victimisation will be upon the person pleading 


it. Since a charge of victimisation is a serious matter reflecting, to a degree, subjective upon the attitude of 
the employer evidenced by acts and conduct, it has to be established by safe and sure evidence. Mere allegations, 
vague suggestions and insinuations are not enough. All particulars of the charge brought out, if believed, must be 
weighed by the Tribunal and a conclusion should be reached on a totality of the evidence produced." 


The Apex Court further held: 


"12. Once, in the opinion of the Tribunal a gross misconduct is established, as required, on legal evidence either in a 
fairly conducted domestic enquiry or before the Tribunal on merits, the plea of victimisation will not carry the case of 
the employee any further. A proved misconduct is antithesis of victimisation as understood in industrial relations." 


13. Thus, in view of the principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court, as discussed above the petitioner workman has 
failed to produce any evidence in support of the plea that the action of Respondent management in dismissing him 
from service is victimization of the petitioner workman. The petitioner workman has failed to discharge his burden of 
proof regarding plea of victimization or unfair labor practices hence same is untenable. 


14. As regard the plea of the petitioner that they he has been acquitted from the criminal trial by court in respect of 
the alleged acts of misconduct. In this context, the decision of Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Deputy 
Inspector General of Police versus Sethu . Thiruvan, 2013 SCC page 598 is relevant, wherein Honorable Apex Court 
have held that mere acquittal in a criminal trial does not nullify or override the finding of a valid domestic inquiry. 
Further, Honorable Apex Court held that the standard of proof in a criminal trial is proof beyond reasonable doubt, 
whereas in a domestic inquiry it is only preponderance of the probability. 


In the case of Commissioner of Police vs Narendra Singh, 2006 SCC page 265, Honorable Apex Court held 
that the disciplinary proceeding can proceed independently and that an employee can be dismissed from service based 
on finding of a department inquiry even if no conviction is recorded in the criminal trial. The finding in the inquiry 
against the workman is based on credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and documentary records and 
same does not warrant any interference. 


15. Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Employers Management West Bokaro Gallery Colly of TISCO Limited 
vs Concern Workman Ram Prakash Singh, 2008 LLR, page 432, 


“16. In U.P State Road Transport Corporation Vinod Kumar, 2007 (13) SCALE 690 this Court again observed that in 
the absence of a challenge to the legality or fairness of the domestic enquiry the Court should be reluctant to either 
interfere with the finding recorded by the Enquiry officer or the punishment awarded by the Punishing Authority. 


17. After going through the order of the industrial Tribunal, were are of the opinion that the Tribunal has interfered 
with the findings recorded by the domestic. Tribunal as if it was the appellate Tribunal. There was evidence present 
on record regarding indecent riotous and disorderly behavior of the Respondent towards his superiors. The 
management witness who were present at the scene of occurrence have unequivocally deposed about the misbehavior 
of the Respondent towards his superiors. Their evidence has been discarded by the Tribunals by observing that in the 
absence of independent evidence, the statements of the workmen who were present at the scene of occurrence could 
not be believed. Industrial Tribunal tell in error in discarding the evidence produce by the management only because 
the independent witnesses were not produce them. It is possible that at the time of occurrence, only the workers of the 
Management and the persons who were truing to put up the constructions dependent evidence was available. 
Statements of the fellow workmen had established the misconduct of the Respondent. Enquiry officer accepted the 
testimony of the witness produced by the management who had clearly implicated the Respondent. It was a legitimate 
conclusion which could be arrived at and it would not be open to the industrial Tribunal to substitute the said opinion 
by its own opinion. 


19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing 
Authority by observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has 
repeatedly had been held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of 
a disciplinary proceeding against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a 
criminal case is different from the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof 
beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : नवम्बर 29, 2025/अग्रहायण 8, 1947 7267 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the 
evidence on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one 
arrived at by the domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal. 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the apex court, as discussed above, the plea of the petitioner that there 
is no legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove 
the guilt of the workman in the alleged misconduct. 


16. Further, as regard the appreciation and evaluation of the evidence in matter of domestic inquiry, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court, in the case of State of Rajasthan and others Vs Him Singh, Civil Appeal Number 3340 of 2020, 
date of decision: 29th October 2021, has laid down the principles extracted as here under: - 


“Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of 
evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a 
criminal trial, of proof be yond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. 
Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the 
spectrum is founded on deference and autonomy -deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact- 
finding authority and autonomy of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. Al the other 
end of the spectrum is the principle that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are 
based on no evidence or when they suffer from perversity. 


To determine whether the finding in a disciplinary inquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of 
scrutiny is undertaken. That is to satisfy the conscience of the courts that there is some evidence to support the charge 
of misconduct and to guard against perversity, but this does not allow the court to re- appreciate evidentiary findings 
in a disciplinary enquiry or to substitute a view which appears lo the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would 
offend the first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense 
without which the judges' craft is in vain.” 


17. In the case of Hombe Gouda Education Trust Vs State of Karnataka, 2006 SCC, page 430: Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held that assaulting a superior at a workplace amount to an act of gross indiscipline. The respondent is a 
teacher. Even under grave provocation, a teacher is not expected to abuse the head of the institution in a filthy 
language and assault him with a chappal. punishment of dismissal from service, therefore, cannot be said to be 
wholly disproportionate so as to shock one's conscience. Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a person, when 
dismissed from service, is put to great hardship, but that would not mean that a grave misconduct (assault on superior 
at workplace) should go unpunished. Maintenance of discipline of an institution is equally important. 


18.Further, In the case of MP Electricity Board Vs Jagdish Sharma, 2005 SCC, page 401, Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held: 


"9. In the case on hand, the employee has been found guilty of hitting and injuring his superior officer at the 
workplace obviously in the breach of Presence of other employees This clearly amounted in an discipline in the 
organisation Discipline at the workplace organisation like the employer herein, is the sine qua non for the efficient 
working of the organisation, when an employee breaches such discipline and the employer terminates his services it 
is not open to a Labour Court of an Industrial Tribunal to take view that the punishment awarded is shockingly 
disproportionate to the charge proved. We have already 


referred to the views of this Court. To quote Jack Chan, 


‘Discipline is a form of civilly responsible behaviour which helps maintain social order and contributes to 
the preservation, if not advancement, of collective interests of society at large.’ 


Obviously, this idea is more relevant in considering the working of an organisation like the employer herein or an 
industrial undertaking. Obedience to authority in a workplace is not slavery. It is rot violative of one's natural rights. It 
is essential for the prosperity of the organisation as well as that of its employee’s. When in such a situation, a 
punishment of termination is awarded for hitting and injuring a superior officer supervising the work of the employee, 
with no extenuating circumstance established, it cannot be said to be not justified. It cannot certainly be termed 
unduly harsh or disproportionate. The Labour Court and the High Court in this case totally misdirected themselves 
while exercising their jurisdiction. The Industrial Court made the correct approach and came to the right conclusion." 


19. Further, in the case of Ajit Kumar Nag Vs Indian Oil Corporation Limited, 2005 SCC page 764, the 
Honorable Supreme Court has held, in a three-judge bench, in paragraph 56, "It is well settled that the burden of 
proving malafide is on the person making the allegation, and the burden is very heavy. There is every presumption in 
favor of the administration that the power has been exercised bona fide and in good faith. It is to be remembered that 
the allegations of malafide are often more easily made than made out, and the very seriousness of such allegations 
demands proof of a high degree of credibility."

Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that assault, intimidation are penal offences. A workman indulging in 
commission of criminal offenses should not be spared only because he happens to be a union leader. The act does not 
encourage indiscipline. It will be a matter of some concern if the opinion of the inquiry officer can be totally ignored, 
despite the fact that the management is precluded from adducing any fresh evidence before the labor court. A union 
leader does not enjoy immunity from being proceeded with in a case of misconduct. 


20. In the case of D. Mulchandani Electric and Radio Industries Limited Vs Workman, 1975 Supreme Court Cases 
page 731, Hon’ble Supreme Court have held: 


establishment 


“Tt was not disputed before us that the allegation of assault, if proved, would be an act subversive of discipline: what 
was contended on behalf of the respondent was between Thana and the premises was that the alleged assault having 
taken place in the train Mulund which was obviously outside the or precincts of the establishment, was not covered by 
Standing Order. 

24(1). The Labour Court also found that the alleged assault did not In our amount to misconduct under Standing 
Order 24(1) which, it was held was restricted to acts and omissions inside the premises of the establish opinion, Lon a 
plain reading of the clause, the words "within the premises or precincts of the establishment" refer not to the place 
where the act which is subversive of discipline or good behaviour is committed but where the consequence of such an 
act manifests itself. In other words, an act, wherever committed, if it has the effect of sub- verting discipline or good 
behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment, will amount to misconduct under Standing Order 
24(1) We are unable to agree that Standing Order 24(1) leaves out of its scone an act committed outside though it may 
result in subversion of discipline or good behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment in question. 
Such a construction in our view would be quite unreasonable.” 


21. In the case of State bank of Bikaner and Jaipur vs Nemi Channel via 2011 Supreme Court cases page 580 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held that subsequent acquittal by criminal court will not in any way render completed 
discipline proceeding invalid, nor affect the validity of finding of the guilt and consequential punishment. 


22. Thus, in view of the foregone discussion and law laid down by the apex court as discussed above, in the instant 
matter all the charges framed and proved in domestic inquiry against the workman being serious and grave in nature 
and stands proved by oral and documentary evidence recorded and produced bin the inquiry. Further, the evidence 
produced by the management before inquiry is legal and admissible as per principle of preponderance of probability 
laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court in its various decisions as discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award. 
Therefore, order of dismissal of Petitioner workman cannot be faulted with, nor it can be said to be in any way 
disproportionate to the gravity of the charges. Thus, the punishment of dismissal of the workman is proportionate to 
the gravity of the charges, and hence deserve to be upheld. Thus, the action of the respondent management in 
dismissing the services of the workman is held legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the workman and in favor of the respondent management. 
Issue No: IV 


In view of foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, II and III, I am of the considered opinion 
that the action of Respondent management in dismissing the Petitioner from service vide order dated 30-08-2016 is 
legal and justified. Therefore, no interference warrants in the punishment of dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 of the 
Petitioner and the action of Respondent Management is held legal and justified and liable to be confirmed. 


AWARD 


In view of the foregone discussion and finding given at issue No. I, II, IIL, and IV, the action of Respondent 
Management in dismissing the service of the Petitioner workman vide order dated 30-08-2016 is held legal and 
justified. Petition filed by the Petitioner sans merit hence dismissed.

Issue No. I

Issue No. वा 


In this context, Respondent No.2 and 3 contended that the present Industrial Dispute has been raised by the 
Petitioner on 2" August 2021 after the lapse of five years from the date of his dismissal order dated 27" May 2016. 
Therefore, in view of the provision contained under section 2-A (3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, this claim could be 
filed by the Petitioner before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or 
otherwise termination of service as specified in (1) of section 2-A. Therefore, the present claim Petition raising the 
Industrial Dispute by Petitioner under section 2A (2) of the ID Act, is barred by limitation. 


The perusal of claim petition goes to reveals that Petitioner has raised the Industrial Dispute against his dismissal 
order, dated 30" august 2016 passed the by the Respondent Management by filing claim petition in the year 2021. In 
the para 11 of claim petition, Petitioner has averred that against his termination order, he approached to the Deputy 
Labour Commissioner of Labor, Nellore for cancellation and same was dismissed without considering the merit. 
Thereafter, he filed petition before Labour court, Guntur, which got registered as ID Number 200/2016. Labour 
Court, Guntur, vide order dated 317 August 2019, has returned his petition on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. 
Thereafter due to COVID-19 pandemic situation Petitioner could not approach this court within time. Petitioner has 
also filed the copy of the order dated 31-08-2019 passed by the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Guntur, in ID no. 
200/2016, whereby Labour Court Guntur has returned petition of the Petitioner for presentation before the appropriate 
court of jurisdiction. It is established fact that in the year 2020, there was a prevailing situation of COVID-19 
pandemic and Petitioner was not able to approach this court to present petition at Hyderabad. Thus, Petitioner has 
furnished cogent and sufficient explanation of delay in filing the present petition and same is not fatal to present 
Industrial Dispute. Therefore, in view of the above present petition raising the Industrial Dispute under section 2-A 
(2) of the ID Act, against the dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 is not barred by limitation. Issue is decided in favor of 
the Petitioner. 


Issue No. III 


The perusal of record goes to reveal that in this claim petition, petitioner has challenged his dismissal order 
dated 30" August 2016, passed by Respondent Management on the grounds alleged in petition. Furthermore, perusal 
of the record of inquiry proceeding along with inquiry report, goes to reveal that the Petitioner was given fair 
opportunity of hearing at every stage of proceedings, which he availed, without raising any objection complaining of 
any prejudice of any nature caused to him before the inquiry officer at any point of time. Further, it is noticed that the 
Workman CSC received all the documents filed and relied upon by the Respondent management in support of the 
charge sheet, and CSC workman also filed a reply, cross-examined the management witnesses, and also examined 
himself as a witness in defense. Thus, the workman CSC has participated in the inquiry proceeding at every stage. 
Inquiry officer, on appreciation of evidence recorded in inquiry has submitted his reasoned report holding the 
workman guilty of the charges. Therefore, in the opinion of the court, no case is made out to hold that the domestic 
inquiry suffers from any procedural lapses or was conducted in violation of principles of natural justice, thereby 
causing any prejudice to the rights of the Petitioner. Moreover, validity and legality of the domestic inquiry has been 
upheld by the court vide order dated 117 November 2024. Thus, the plea of the Petitioner that the domestic inquiry 
was conducted against the Petitioner in violation of principle of natural justice is untenable.

squarely fall under the category of serious misconduct as defined under Clauses 19(a), (c), (d) and (e) of the Andhra

Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is 
not condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and 
appropriate action.

dealt with strictly and are not open to lenient treatment. The reinstatement ordered by the Labour Court was 
reversed, affirming the employer's authority to maintain discipline through dismissal. 


(9) In the case of Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka - (2006) 1 


SSC 430, the Hon’ble Supreme Court underscored the importance of workplace discipline and held that even 
provoked assault on a superior, amounts to gross indiscipline. The Court stated: "30. In view of the change in 
economic policy of the country, it may not now be proper to allow the employees to break the discipline with 
impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with 
law.” 


(f) In the case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd - (2008) 5 SCC 554, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and 
Rubber Co. Vs. The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere 
therewith. In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to 
a conclusion that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested 
otherwise but it is another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere 
hypothesis. It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the 
Act although is a wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and 
analyze the evidence but what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal 
and proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman 
had Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, 
which was awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the 
punishment was awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record." 


(g) The Supreme Court in the case of Northeastern Karnataka RTC Vs. Ashappa 2006 (5) SCC 137 reaffirmed 
that the Tribunal must not lightly interfere with the employer's disciplinary decisions and reiterated the "shockingly 
disproportionate" standard. 


(h) In Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka (cupra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
clarified that the days of automatic sympathy towards the workman are over, and that discipline must be maintained at 
all costs in light of contemporary industrial conditions. The Tribunal's power to substitute the employer's decision 
must be exercised with restraint. 


(i) In the case of Muriadih Colliery (Supra) & Krishnakali Tea 


Estate (Supra), the Apex Court expressly held that interference by Labour Courts with dismissal orders passed for 
acts involving violence and assault was not permissible under section 11-A of the ID Act, as the punishment was not 
disproportionate. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Honorable Apex Court as discussed above, there is ample 
oral and documentary evidence on record to substantiate the charges against the petitioner workman, and it cannot be 
said that the order of dismissal of Petitioner is perverse or shockingly disproportionate. 


12. As regard the plea of the petitioner workman that Respondent Management has victimize him due to the being 
member of the union and also for raising the demand related to welfare of the workman.

In this context, Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Iron 
Works versus Bhagobhai Balubhai Patel, 1976 SCC page 518. Therein Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
legal test for establishing the plea of victimization as discussed here under: - 


"11. The onus of establishing plea of victimisation will be upon the person pleading 


it. Since a charge of victimisation is a serious matter reflecting, to a degree, subjective upon the attitude of 
the employer evidenced by acts and conduct, it has to be established by safe and sure evidence. Mere allegations, 
vague suggestions and insinuations are not enough. All particulars of the charge brought out, if believed, must be 
weighed by the Tribunal and a conclusion should be reached on a totality of the evidence produced." 


The Apex Court further held: 


"12. Once, in the opinion of the Tribunal a gross misconduct is established, as required, on legal evidence either in a 
fairly conducted domestic enquiry or before the Tribunal on merits, the plea of victimisation will not carry the case of 
the employee any further. A proved misconduct is antithesis of victimisation as understood in industrial relations." 


13. Thus, in view of the principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court, as discussed above the petitioner workman has 
failed to produce any evidence in support of the plea that the action of Respondent management in dismissing him 
from service is victimization of the petitioner workman. The petitioner workman has failed to discharge his burden of 
proof regarding plea of victimization or unfair labor practices hence same is untenable.

the alleged acts of misconduct. In this context, the decision of Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Deputy 
Inspector General of Police versus Sethu . Thiruvan, 2013 SCC page 598 is relevant, wherein Honorable Apex Court 
have held that mere acquittal in a criminal trial does not nullify or override the finding of a valid domestic inquiry. 
Further, Honorable Apex Court held that the standard of proof in a criminal trial is proof beyond reasonable doubt, 
whereas in a domestic inquiry it is only preponderance of the probability. 


In the case of Commissioner of Police vs Narendra Singh, 2006 SCC page 265, Honorable Apex Court held 
that the disciplinary proceeding can proceed independently and that an employee can be dismissed from service based 
on finding of a department inquiry even if no conviction is recorded in the criminal trial. The finding in the inquiry 
against the workman is based on credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and documentary records and 
same does not warrant any interference. 


15. Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Employers Management West Bokaro Gallery Colly of TISCO Limited 
vs Concern Workman Ram Prakash Singh, 2008 LLR, page 432, 


“16. In U.P State Road Transport Corporation Vinod Kumar, 2007 (13) SCALE 690 this Court again observed that in 
the absence of a challenge to the legality or fairness of the domestic enquiry the Court should be reluctant to either 
interfere with the finding recorded by the Enquiry officer or the punishment awarded by the Punishing Authority. 


17. After going through the order of the industrial Tribunal, were are of the opinion that the Tribunal has interfered 
with the findings recorded by the domestic. Tribunal as if it was the appellate Tribunal. There was evidence present 
on record regarding indecent riotous and disorderly behavior of the Respondent towards his superiors. The 
management witness who were present at the scene of occurrence have unequivocally deposed about the misbehavior 
of the Respondent towards his superiors. Their evidence has been discarded by the Tribunals by observing that in the 
absence of independent evidence, the statements of the workmen who were present at the scene of occurrence could 
not be believed. Industrial Tribunal tell in error in discarding the evidence produce by the management only because 
the independent witnesses were not produce them. It is possible that at the time of occurrence, only the workers of the 
Management and the persons who were truing to put up the constructions dependent evidence was available. 
Statements of the fellow workmen had established the misconduct of the Respondent. Enquiry officer accepted the 
testimony of the witness produced by the management who had clearly implicated the Respondent. It was a legitimate 
conclusion which could be arrived at and it would not be open to the industrial Tribunal to substitute the said opinion 
by its own opinion. 


19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing 
Authority by observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has 
repeatedly had been held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of 
a disciplinary proceeding against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a 
criminal case is different from the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof 
beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the 
evidence on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one 
arrived at by the domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal.

Thus, in view of the law laid down by the apex court, as discussed above, the plea of the petitioner that there 
is no legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove 
the guilt of the workman in the alleged misconduct. 


16. Further, as regard the appreciation and evaluation of the evidence in matter of domestic inquiry, Hon’ble 
Supreme Court, in the case of State of Rajasthan and others Vs Him Singh, Civil Appeal Number 3340 of 2020, 
date of decision: 29th October 2021, has laid down the principles extracted as here under: - 


“Disciplinary enquiries have to abide by the rules of natural justice. But they are not governed by strict rules of 
evidence which apply to judicial proceedings. The standard of proof is hence not the strict standard which governs a 
criminal trial, of proof be yond reasonable doubt, but a civil standard governed by a preponderance of probabilities. 
Within the rule of preponderance, there are varying approaches based on context and subject. The first end of the 
spectrum is founded on deference and autonomy -deference to the position of the disciplinary authority as a fact- 
finding authority and autonomy of the employer in maintaining discipline and efficiency of the service. Al the other 
end of the spectrum is the principle that the court has the jurisdiction to interfere when the findings in the enquiry are 
based on no evidence or when they suffer from perversity. 


To determine whether the finding in a disciplinary inquiry is based on some evidence an initial or threshold level of 
scrutiny is undertaken. That is to satisfy the conscience of the courts that there is some evidence to support the charge 
of misconduct and to guard against perversity, but this does not allow the court to re- appreciate evidentiary findings 
in a disciplinary enquiry or to substitute a view which appears lo the judge to be more appropriate. To do so would 
offend the first principle which has been outlined above. The ultimate guide is the exercise of robust common sense 
without which the judges' craft is in vain.” 


17. In the case of Hombe Gouda Education Trust Vs State of Karnataka, 2006 SCC, page 430: Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held that assaulting a superior at a workplace amount to an act of gross indiscipline. The respondent is a 
teacher. Even under grave provocation, a teacher is not expected to abuse the head of the institution in a filthy 
language and assault him with a chappal. punishment of dismissal from service, therefore, cannot be said to be 
wholly disproportionate so as to shock one's conscience. Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a person, when 
dismissed from service, is put to great hardship, but that would not mean that a grave misconduct (assault on superior 
at workplace) should go unpunished. Maintenance of discipline of an institution is equally important. 


18.Further, In the case of MP Electricity Board Vs Jagdish Sharma, 2005 SCC, page 401, Hon’ble Supreme Court 
have held: 


"9. In the case on hand, the employee has been found guilty of hitting and injuring his superior officer at the 
workplace obviously in the breach of Presence of other employees This clearly amounted in an discipline in the 
organisation Discipline at the workplace organisation like the employer herein, is the sine qua non for the efficient 
working of the organisation, when an employee breaches such discipline and the employer terminates his services it 
is not open to a Labour Court of an Industrial Tribunal to take view that the punishment awarded is shockingly 
disproportionate to the charge proved. We have already 


referred to the views of this Court. To quote Jack Chan, 


‘Discipline is a form of civilly responsible behaviour which helps maintain social order and contributes to 
the preservation, if not advancement, of collective interests of society at large.’ 


Obviously, this idea is more relevant in considering the working of an organisation like the employer herein or an 
industrial undertaking. Obedience to authority in a workplace is not slavery. It is rot violative of one's natural rights. It 
is essential for the prosperity of the organisation as well as that of its employee’s. When in such a situation, a 
punishment of termination is awarded for hitting and injuring a superior officer supervising the work of the employee, 
with no extenuating circumstance established, it cannot be said to be not justified. It cannot certainly be termed 
unduly harsh or disproportionate. The Labour Court and the High Court in this case totally misdirected themselves 
while exercising their jurisdiction. The Industrial Court made the correct approach and came to the right conclusion." 


19. Further, in the case of Ajit Kumar Nag Vs Indian Oil Corporation Limited, 2005 SCC page 764, the 
Honorable Supreme Court has held, in a three-judge bench, in paragraph 56, "It is well settled that the burden of 
proving malafide is on the person making the allegation, and the burden is very heavy. There is every presumption in 
favor of the administration that the power has been exercised bona fide and in good faith. It is to be remembered that 
the allegations of malafide are often more easily made than made out, and the very seriousness of such allegations 
demands proof of a high degree of credibility." 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court held that assault, intimidation are penal offences. A workman indulging in 
commission of criminal offenses should not be spared only because he happens to be a union leader. The act does not 
encourage indiscipline. It will be a matter of some concern if the opinion of the inquiry officer can be totally ignored, 
despite the fact that the management is precluded from adducing any fresh evidence before the labor court. A union 
leader does not enjoy immunity from being proceeded with in a case of misconduct.

Standing Order. 


24(1). The Labour Court also found that the alleged assault did not In our amount to misconduct under Standing 
Order 24(1) which, it was held was restricted to acts and omissions inside the premises of the establish opinion, Lon a 
plain reading of the clause, the words "within the premises or precincts of the establishment" refer not to the place 
where the act which is subversive of discipline or good behaviour is committed but where the consequence of such an 
act manifests itself. In other words, an act, wherever committed, if it has the effect of sub- verting discipline or good 
behaviour within the premises or precincts of the establishment, will amount to misconduct under Standing Order

22. Thus, in view of the foregone discussion and law laid down by the apex court as discussed above, in the instant 
matter all the charges framed and proved in domestic inquiry against the workman being serious and grave in nature 
and stands proved by oral and documentary evidence recorded and produced bin the inquiry. Further, the evidence 
produced by the management before inquiry is legal and admissible as per principle of preponderance of probability 
laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court in its various decisions as discussed in preceding paragraph of this Award. 
Therefore, order of dismissal of Petitioner workman cannot be faulted with, nor it can be said to be in any way 
disproportionate to the gravity of the charges. Thus, the punishment of dismissal of the workman is proportionate to 
the gravity of the charges, and hence deserve to be upheld. Thus, the action of the respondent management in 
dismissing the services of the workman is held legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the workman and in favor of the respondent management.

Findings: - 
Issue No. I 


The Departmental inquiry conducted against the Workman Sri. Daggu Sathish has been held legal and valid,

Issue No. II 


In this context, Respondent No.2 and 3 contended that the present Industrial Dispute has been raised by the 
Petitioner on 2" August 2021 after the lapse of five years from the date of his dismissal order dated 27" May 2016. 
Therefore, in view of the provision contained under section 2-A (3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, this claim could be 
filed by the Petitioner before the expiry of three years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or 
otherwise termination of service as specified in (1) of section 2-A. Therefore, the present claim Petition raising the 
Industrial Dispute by Petitioner under section 2A (2) of the ID Act, is barred by limitation. 


The perusal of claim petition goes to reveals that Petitioner has raised the Industrial Dispute against his dismissal 
order, dated 30" august 2016 passed the by the Respondent Management by filing claim petition in the year 2021. In 
the para 11 of claim petition, Petitioner has averred that against his termination order, he approached to the Deputy 
Labour Commissioner of Labor, Nellore for cancellation and same was dismissed without considering the merit. 
Thereafter, he filed petition before Labour court, Guntur, which got registered as ID Number 203/2016. Labour 
Court, Guntur, vide order dated 317 August 2019, has returned his petition on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. 
Thereafter due to COVID-19 pandemic situation Petitioner could not approach this court within time. Petitioner has 
also filed the copy of the order dated 31-08-2019 passed by the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Guntur, in ID no. 
203/2016, whereby Labour Court Guntur has returned petition of the Petitioner for presentation before the appropriate 
court of jurisdiction. It is established fact that in the year 2020, there was a prevailing situation of COVID-19 
pandemic and Petitioner was not able to approach this court to present petition at Hyderabad. Thus, Petitioner has 
furnished cogent and sufficient explanation of delay in filing the present petition and same is not fatal to present 
Industrial Dispute. Therefore, in view of the above present petition raising the Industrial Dispute under section 2-A 
(2) of the ID Act, against the dismissal order dated 30-08-2016 is not barred by limitation. Issue is decided in favor of 
the Petitioner. 


Issue No. III 


The perusal of record goes to reveal that in this claim petition, petitioner has challenged his dismissal order 
dated 307 August 2016, passed by Respondent Management on the grounds alleged in petition. Furthermore, perusal 
of the record of inquiry proceeding along with inquiry report, goes to reveal that the Petitioner was given fair 
opportunity of hearing at every stage of proceedings, which he availed, without raising any objection complaining of 
any prejudice of any nature caused to him before the inquiry officer at any point of time. Further, it is noticed that the 
Workman CSC received all the documents filed and relied upon by the Respondent management in support of the 
charge sheet, and CSC workman also filed a reply, cross-examined the management witnesses, and also examined 
himself as a witness in defense. Thus, the workman CSC has participated in the inquiry proceeding at every stage. 
Inquiry officer, on appreciation of evidence recorded in inquiry has submitted his reasoned report holding the 
workman guilty of the charges. Therefore, in the opinion of the court, no case is made out to hold that the domestic 
inquiry suffers from any procedural lapses or was conducted in violation of principles of natural justice, thereby 
causing any prejudice to the rights of the Petitioner. Moreover, validity and legality of the domestic inquiry has been 
upheld by the court vide order dated 11" November 2024. Thus, the plea of the Petitioner that the domestic inquiry 
was conducted against the Petitioner in violation of principle of natural justice is untenable. 


It is settled law that once it is held that the domestic inquiry is legal and proper, the next question arises for

Rules 19 (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of AP Shops & Establishment Rules provides as here under: - 

i. Clause 19(a): Willful insubordination or disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of a superior. 
ii. Clause 19(C): Damage to the employer’s property. 

iii. Clause 19(d): Riotous or disorderly behavior in the premises of the establishment. 

iv. Clause 19(e): Threatening or intimidating any employee or superior. 


The misconduct committed by the workman along with employees of assaulting superiors, instigating others, and 
participating in the riotous violent activities constitute serious act of misconduct which strike at the root of workplace 
discipline. The act of workman causing grievous injuries to managerial staff is a grave and serious misconduct that is 
not condonable. Therefore, the dismissal order passed by Respondent against the workman is justified and 
appropriate action.

(c) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M.P, Electricity Board Vs. Jagdish Chandra Sharma - order (2005)

dealt with strictly and are not open to lenient treatment. The reinstatement ordered by the Labour Court was 
reversed, affirming the employer's authority to maintain discipline through dismissal. 


(d) In the case of Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka - (2006) 1 


SSC 430, the Hon’ble Supreme Court underscored the importance of workplace discipline and held that even 
provoked assault on a superior, amounts to gross indiscipline. The Court stated: "30. In view of the change in 
economic policy of the country, it may not now be proper to allow the employees to break the discipline with 
impunity. Our country is governed by the rule of law. All actions, therefore, must be taken in accordance with 
law.” 


(e) In the case of Usha Breco Mazdoor Sangh Vs. Management of M/S. Usha Breco Ltd - (2008) 5 SCC 554, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court while reaffirming the legal position laid down by it is in the case firestone Tyre and 
Rubber Co. Vs. The management and Others — (1973) 1 SCC 813, held: - 


“31. It is one thing to say that finding of an Enquiry Officer is perverse or betrays the well-known doctrine of 
proportionality another thing to say that only because two views are possible, the Labour Court shall interfere 
therewith. In other words, it is one thing to say that on the basis of the materials on record, the Labour Court comes to 
a conclusion that a verdict of guilt has been arrived at by the Enquiry Officer whereas the materials suggested 
otherwise but it is another thing to say that such a verdict was also a possible view. 


39. The upshot of our discussion is that the decision of the labour Court should not be based on mere 
hypothesis. It cannot overturn a decision of the Management on ipse dixit. Its jurisdiction under section 11-A of the 
Act although is a wide one, must be judiciously exercise either whimsically or capriciously. It may scrutinize and 
analyze the evidence but what is important is how it does so.” 


(f) Further, in the case of New Shorrock Mills vs Maheshbhai T. Rao, 1996 SCC page 590. Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held: - 


“35. In the case of New Shorrock Mills Vs. (1996) Maheshbhai T Rao 6 of SCC 590, held that: 


"Labour Court in the present case having come to a Conclusion that the finding of the departmental enquiry was legal 
and proper, the Respondents order of discharge was not by way of victimization and that the Respondent workman 
had Seriously misbehaved and was thus guilty of misconduct, ought not to have interfered with the punishment, 
which was awarded, in the manner it did. This is not a case where the Court Could Come to the conclusion that the 
punishment was awarded was shockingly disproportionate to the employee's conduct and his past service record." 


(g) The Supreme Court in the case of Northeastern Karnataka RTC Vs. Ashappa 2006 (5) SCC 137 reaffirmed 
that the Tribunal must not lightly interfere with the employer's disciplinary decisions and reiterated the "shockingly 
disproportionate" standard. 


(h) In Hombe Gowda Educational Trust Vs. State of Karnataka (cupra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
clarified that the days of automatic sympathy towards the workman are over, and that discipline must be maintained at 
all costs in light of contemporary industrial conditions. The Tribunal's power to substitute the employer's decision 
must be exercised with restraint. 


(i) In the case of Muriadih Colliery (Supra) & Krishnakali Tea 


Estate (Supra), the Apex Court expressly held that interference by Labour Courts with dismissal orders passed for 
acts involving violence and assault was not permissible under section 11-A of the ID Act, as the punishment was not 
disproportionate. 


Thus, in view of the principles laid down by the Honorable Apex Court as discussed above, there is ample 
oral and documentary evidence on record to substantiate the charges against the petitioner workman, and it cannot be 
said that the order of dismissal of Petitioner is perverse or shockingly disproportionate. 


12. As regard the plea of the petitioner workman that Respondent Management has victimize him due to the being 
member of the union and also for raising the demand related to welfare of the workman. 


In this context, Respondent has relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Iron 
Works versus Bhagobhai Balubhai Patel, 1976 SCC page 518. Therein Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
legal test for establishing the plea of victimization as discussed here under: - 


7290 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA NOVEMBER 29, 2025/AGRAHAY ANA 8, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


"11. The onus of establishing plea of victimisation will be upon the person pleading 


it. Since a charge of victimisation is a serious matter reflecting, to a degree, subjective upon the attitude of 
the employer evidenced by acts and conduct, it has to be established by safe and sure evidence. Mere allegations, 
vague suggestions and insinuations are not enough. All particulars of the charge brought out, if believed, must be 
weighed by the Tribunal and a conclusion should be reached on a totality of the evidence produced." 


The Apex Court further held: 


"12. Once, in the opinion of the Tribunal a gross misconduct is established, as required, on legal evidence either in a 
fairly conducted domestic enquiry or before the Tribunal on merits, the plea of victimisation will not carry the case of 
the employee any further. A proved misconduct is antithesis of victimisation as understood in industrial relations." 


13. Thus, in view of the principle laid down by Hon’ble Apex Court, as discussed above the petitioner workman has 
failed to produce any evidence in support of the plea that the action of Respondent management in dismissing him 
from service is victimization of the petitioner workman. The petitioner workman has failed to discharge his burden of 
proof regarding plea of victimization or unfair labor practices hence same is untenable. 


14. As regard the plea of the petitioner that they he has been acquitted from the criminal trial by court in respect of 
the alleged acts of misconduct. In this context, the decision of Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Deputy 
Inspector General of Police versus Sethu . Thiruvan, 2013 SCC page 598 is relevant, wherein Honorable Apex Court 
have held that mere acquittal in a criminal trial does not nullify or override the finding of a valid domestic inquiry. 
Further, Honorable Apex Court held that the standard of proof in a criminal trial is proof beyond reasonable doubt, 
whereas in a domestic inquiry it is only preponderance of the probability. 


In the case of Commissioner of Police vs Narendra Singh, 2006 SCC page 265, Honorable Apex Court held 
that the disciplinary proceeding can proceed independently and that an employee can be dismissed from service based 
on finding of a department inquiry even if no conviction is recorded in the criminal trial. The finding in the inquiry 
against the workman is based on credible evidence, including eyewitness testimonies and documentary records and 
same does not warrant any interference. 


15. Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Employers Management West Bokaro Gallery Colly of TISCO Limited 
vs Concern Workman Ram Prakash Singh, 2008 LLR, page 432, 


“16. In U.P State Road Transport Corporation Vinod Kumar, 2007 (13) SCALE 690 this Court again observed that in 
the absence of a challenge to the legality or fairness of the domestic enquiry the Court should be reluctant to either 
interfere with the finding recorded by the Enquiry officer or the punishment awarded by the Punishing Authority. 


17. After going through the order of the industrial Tribunal, were are of the opinion that the Tribunal has interfered 
with the findings recorded by the domestic. Tribunal as if it was the appellate Tribunal. There was evidence present 
on record regarding indecent riotous and disorderly behavior of the Respondent towards his superiors. The 
management witness who were present at the scene of occurrence have unequivocally deposed about the misbehavior 
of the Respondent towards his superiors. Their evidence has been discarded by the Tribunals by observing that in the 
absence of independent evidence, the statements of the workmen who were present at the scene of occurrence could 
not be believed. Industrial Tribunal tell in error in discarding the evidence produce by the management only because 
the independent witnesses were not produce them. It is possible that at the time of occurrence, only the workers of the 
Management and the persons who were truing to put up the constructions dependent evidence was available. 
Statements of the fellow workmen had established the misconduct of the Respondent. Enquiry officer accepted the 
testimony of the witness produced by the management who had clearly implicated the Respondent. It was a legitimate 
conclusion which could be arrived at and it would not be open to the industrial Tribunal to substitute the said opinion 
by its own opinion. 


19. Tribunal has set aside the report of the enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal passed by the punishing 
Authority by observing that the charges against the Respondent were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. It has 
repeatedly had been held by the court that the acquittal in a criminal case could not operate as a bar for drawing up of 
a disciplinary proceeding against a delinquent. It is well settled principle of law that yardstick and standard proof in a 
criminal case is different from the one disciplinary proceeding. While the standard of proof in a criminal case is proof 
beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof in a departmental proceeding is preponderance of probabilities.” 


Further, the Honorable Supreme Court has observed that in a case where two views are possible on the 
evidence on record, then the Industrial Tribunal should be very slow in coming to a conclusion other than the one 
arrived at by the domestic Tribunal, by substituting its opinion in place of the opinion of the domestic tribunal. 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by the apex court, as discussed above, the plea of the petitioner that there 
is no legal evidence on record is untenable, as there is sufficient evidence on record of the domestic inquiry to prove 
the guilt of the workman in the alleged misconduct.
